A single pale silver channel enters the left edge low, makes a long shallow bend and leaves near the upper right. A hairline tributary branches inside its elbow. Black-violet silt fills most of the sheet. At lower right a thumb-sized island of ochre salt grass pins the large empty field. Raking light from the far side raises each little ripple on one bank; the other bank falls into plum shadow. The sheltered water reads as flat tarnished pewter. The camera is exactly parallel to the mud, close enough to resolve little combs of sand. Cold restrained colour, a quiet expanse all the way to the edges.
images.note: The salt island gives this quiet sheet a second scale. The original panoramic study has a stronger double bend; this print uses the full shop ratio.

images.title: The Red Hull
images.prompt: A horizontal oil painting of a boat hull seen from water level in a working harbour. A great vermilion bow enters from the upper left, cropped so decisively that its sloping side becomes a wedge. Its narrow black waterline crosses the centre before doubling back as a red reflection cut by the swell. Cold mint water takes the right two thirds. Far along its top edge a low grey quay is just a few blunt brushstrokes. Paint builds up thickly against the edge of the hull, drags dry over the primed surface of the water, and breaks into little flicks of pale primer on the nearest wave. All marks come from a loaded palette knife or a flat bristle brush, across the entire surface. An intimate view painted from a low boat, without lettering or frame.
images.note: The simplest version wins at viewing distance. The reflection supplies a second, softer edge to the same bow, and muted white lets that relationship hold.
